It still asserts "No past runs yet" between mount and the first fetch resolving, because sessions starts [] and sessionsFailed starts false — indistinguishable from a completed empty load. Three states exist in reality (unknown, empty, failed); the UI models two. Self-corrects in about a second, so far less costly than #72's version — but the *same missing distinction*, found in the code that had just been fixed for its sibling

A value correct in the context it was written for shipped into another where it reads as broken, and only a browser could show it. _derive_title trims to 60 characters — right for a ~180px sidebar column, inherited unexamined by a ~1170px full-width tile, where the text fills a third of the space and stops mid-phrase. Every test passed; none could have caught it, because the defect is entirely in the relationship between a number and a layout. Flagged as an open question in the plan, built to the default when the question went unanswered, and the default turned out to be wrong in a way only visible once rendered
surfacedIn: biffo-plugin-ideation report tile, seen on dev

summary: A single-page app that authorises requests from a session object captured at mount stops working silently at token expiry. A CognitoUserSession is an immutable snapshot: getIdToken() returns the same token forever, and getCurrentSession() hands back the *cached* one whose isValid() is true right up to the expiry second. So a page that mounts with seconds of token life left 401s every subsequent call for the rest of its life — no signed-out state, no retry, no recovery but a reload the user has no reason to attempt. Found in the founder app and then, identically, in the admin panel beside it

RECURRENCE, third instance: a list that renders "loaded but empty" and "failed to load" as the same state turns any staleness or auth failure into an apparent data-loss report. Already recorded twice — an admin panel showing a 500 as "No catalog entries yet", then the same shape in another repo. This one is the most expensive yet: "No past runs yet" was reported as lost sessions, twice, and each report came with a confident and wrong diagnosis (first "the list endpoint is broken", then "four Cognito pools make identity vary by page load"). Two sessions searched two wrong layers because the UI asserted a fact it could not know. The condition is not a UI-copy problem, it is a UI that has no representation for "I don't know"

A list refreshed only on a downstream success event goes permanently stale when that event never fires. refreshSessions() ran at mount, on report materialisation and after a delete — never after the create that produced the row. A run created on a page whose list predated it stayed invisible for that page's entire life while returning 200 to any direct call, and the report poll's catch stopped the poll permanently, removing the last remaining refresh path. The create path must refresh what it creates; hanging it off a later success couples visibility to a step that may never happen

A test can pin an agreement between two values, neither of which reaches a request. test_the_reported_models_are_the_models_the_founder_app_uses asserted builtin_chat_agents()["challenger"]["model"] == app._CHAT_MODEL. Both were real, both were equal, and both were discarded before the wire — the plugin sent Core no chat model at all. The guard was green for the whole life of the defect it was named after. Condition: a drift guard compares two sources without any assertion that either is consumed

A gate can pass while structurally unable to observe the thing it guards. test_costs_no_core_round_trip enforced that /effective-config made no call to Core. The property wanted was "cannot fail when Core is cold"; what it encoded was "must not look" — and a route that must not look cannot be correct about anything stored. Condition: a test asserts the absence of a mechanism as a proxy for a guarantee that mechanism could still have provided

Two panels answered the same question from different sources and only one consulted the authority. The Chat Agents tab read stored rows and labelled them honestly; the Model Catalog tab's "Models in use" block reported built-in constants as though they were in use. Same page, same session, opposite answers — and the constant it reported could never affect a request, so this was not stale configuration but a display fiction. effective_config's own docstring asserted a fallback that did not exist

Authentication runs before routing, so from outside a deployment a plugin that does not exist is indistinguishable from a live one. Verifying an install, /api/v1/plugins/idea-scout/build-types returned 401 — and so did /api/v1/plugins/does-not-exist-xyz/foo. Four 401s read as confirmation until a deliberately-absent control was added. Nothing externally observable answers "is this plugin mounted?", which is the exact question every install verification asks

A pre-push gate reported verify passed on a change written entirely in a language it never checked. In a plugin repo it printed javascript n/a - no package.json in this repo — true of the repo *root*, while the change was 100% TypeScript under web-admin/. The same gate in an instance, which has a root package.json, ran lint, typecheck, formatcheck and test on the same kind of change. Condition: a gate detects applicability from a marker at the repo root, in repos whose code deliberately does not live there — so the language most plugin changes are written in is the one least verified, in green

RECURRENCE of a condition this project has written down twice and warns about in AGENTS.md §6: a piped git push reports the pipe's status, so a failed push prints success. I ran git push -q ... 2>&1 | grep -v vulnerabilit | tail -1; echo "push: $?" and got push: 0 while the push had failed and the commit had never been made — lint-staged was missing because I skipped the worktree's pnpm install. It surfaced only because gh pr create refused for want of a remote branch. The rule was quoted earlier in the same session by the same author. Condition: a safety rule that depends on remembering not to pipe will be violated by anyone filtering noisy output — and both times, the noise being filtered was unrelated (a dependabot banner)
fixesIn: biffo-template — the rule needs a mechanism, not a reminder

summary: RECURRENCE, and a new shape: complete-but-open reached the parent. Three more instances in one day — an epic, a milestone, and a delivered API issue. The epic's own checklist had all nine boxes unticked against eight closed milestones, so it asserted "nothing delivered" throughout a completed v1. Nothing ticks a parent when a child closes and nothing compares the two, so the tracker's summary view degrades in exactly the direction that hides finished work. Previously recorded at the leaf; this is the first at the roll-up that people actually read

Rewording a scoreboard row silently duplicates it in the dataset. Row identity is derived from the row's own text, and mergeExtracted keeps orphans, so an edited row is stored as a *new* row while the pre-edit version survives — every correction inflates the corpus. I did it three times in one session correcting my own figures, publishing a headline of 161 against a page rendering 157. The retention is deliberate and load-bearing: dropping orphans previously deleted every stored row a stale branch's markdown did not mention, and that fired for real. So this is a genuine trade-off between silent duplication and silent deletion, not a bug with an obvious side — and nothing currently reports either number against the other
fixesIn: biffo-template — needs a decision, not a patch

summary: 51 of 155 rows have no date, so a third of the corpus cannot be time-sliced. "Is this class getting better or worse?" is unanswerable for those rows, and they are silently excluded from any windowed view rather than reported as missing

The effort log cannot be sliced by repo: 10 of 26 entries — 1,200m, 36% of one day's logged minutes — name no repo. The dashboard's per-repo platform/product split is inferred from commit types and repo names, and the recorded entries exist to falsify that inference. Entries naming no repo cannot confirm or refute it, so a third of the ground truth is inert against the thing it was collected for

Three repos merged work with no effort entry at all — biffo-plugins-registry (4 PRs), biffo-platform-app (1), tabsii-intake (1). Not proof of unlogged effort: a repo can take a merge carried from elsewhere. But nothing distinguishes "no effort spent here" from "effort spent and not logged", so the zero cannot be read either way
surfacedIn: estate-wide, measured across 145 merges in one day

summary: 26 of 155 rows sit at status unfiled: recorded as findings with no issue raised and therefore no route to action. They are counted in every headline the scoreboard produces, so the corpus reports a level of engagement the backlog does not carry

A new guard's ZERO is a claim about the world, and the first version of this one was structurally incapable of finding the defect it was written for. The class is *"an RLS-gated row is invisible on this session, and invisible is indistinguishable from absent"* — this page's own most-repeated finding. The obvious check is *does a policy pass NULL for a scope the TABLE has a column for*, and it reported 0 of 152 policies. Not a clean bill of health: media_assets has no brand_id column at all, so it could never have caught media_assets.create, the known-true case that motivated it. Reported rather than interrogated, a guard that finds nothing would have shipped as proof the class was closed — a fail-open in the very mechanism built to end fail-opens. The working relationship is one level up: between the scope_level of the roles holding a permission and the scope arguments its policies pass. The rule this suggests: a new guard is not trusted until it has been run against a known-true instance and failed. Both guards in #440 were finally proven by mutation, not by passing

A long-lived local database drifts in two directions at once, and neither is visible from a query. The RLS grant sweep was first run against a lane container left up for 33 hours. It predated 063_audit_logs_brand_scoping.sql — the module that *fixed* audit_logs.read — so the audit reported a defect that had already shipped a fix, and the whole 49-item baseline described a schema that no longer existed. Caught only by reading db/imports/ and noticing a filename that described the finding being reported. Then the opposite: verifying the guard against that same database took it from 5 seeded roles to 148, because the DDL seeds exactly one tenant and every other role is created by a *test*. So the same query before and after the suite gives different answers, with nothing indicating why. Behind the DDL, and ahead of it by residue. Nothing stamps a lane database with the DDL revision it was built from
fixesIn: not fixed — candidates: build into a throwaway database per run, or record the highest applied module and refuse a stale one

summary: A guard that reads runtime state in a shared-database lane is order-dependent until proven otherwise, and "it passed when I ran it" is not that proof. The grant-satisfiability check passed run alone and failed on the full lane, reporting three findings that were test fixtures — test_marketplace_media.py builds a region-scoped role holding brand_media.read to exercise one policy, which is legitimate. Keying findings on (permission_code, scope_level) rather than role name was not enough, because a fixture can invent a genuinely new pair. Fixed by confining the guard to the DDL-seeded tenant, plus an assertion naming the four roles it must find so a re-seed or rename fails loudly instead of quietly shrinking what is examined. This lane deliberately runs the whole suite twice against one database, so residue is guaranteed rather than hypothetical — and every existing guard that queries application tables inherits this exposure
fixesIn: tabsii-platform #440 — scoped to the seeded tenant; 253 passed twice

summary: The estate's own escalation guard was satisfied by zero as readily as by one. chk_ura_one_level on user_role_assignments reads num_nonnulls(brand_id, region_id, unit_id, franchisee_id) <= 1 — which permits none set, the tenant-wide shape. fn_authorized's first branch matches when all four are NULL and does not inspect the passed scope arguments at all, so a role declared scope_level = 'brand' assigned that way matched every row in the tenant, for every permission it held, while whoami reported the role's intended shape. Found incidentally while building an unrelated guard, not by any audit. The declarative fix is a composite FK, and it was built and then rejected: MATCH SIMPLE skips enforcement entirely when any referencing column is NULL, so it would have been a fail-open inside the guard — and closing that needs a NOT NULL that rejects live rows. A trigger has neither problem. Worth asking of every <= in a constraint in this estate: is zero a legal answer, and did anyone mean it to be?
fixesIn: tabsii-platform #440 — DDL module 070, deployed to dev (applied: ["070_ura_scope_matches_role.sql"])

summary: Recording the choice before building is not sufficient to avoid a false did not move — the tool produces one by a second route. /practices-standup's loop closure fires on any prior entry regardless of whether a new snapshot has been collected since, so a choice recorded the same morning as the snapshot it was read from is scored against its own baseline and the delta is 0 by construction. Observed 2026-07-31: choice chosenAt 04:22Z, snapshot generatedAt 03:39Z, same file, printed 16.8 → 16.8 did not move (0) and labelled it *"Yesterday you chose"*. The metric had in fact moved 29.6 → 16.8 (-43%), and even that was not attributable because the intervention post-dated the collection — the honest verdict was *too early*. The skill is emphatic about the ordering rule and that rule was followed; the guidance is therefore incomplete rather than ignored. A did not move is meant to be the most valuable signal this process produces, and one that fires on a self-comparison trains the reader to discount all of them. A delta of exactly 0 deserves the same suspicion as a zero row count
fixesIn: biffo-template #1037 — refuse to score a choice whose chosenAt is at or after the snapshot's generatedAt

summary: Nothing at filing time says which repo owns the code a symptom appears in, so a backlog fills with issues its own repo cannot action. Six of eleven open instance issues had their fix in a template-owned path. Two of the six state their own template ownership in the body and were filed downstream regardless; one was raised against an instance it had not even surfaced in, in a repo with almost no other traffic, where nobody would have found it. This is not carelessness — an issue is filed where the symptom appeared, which is the only thing the reporter knows, and the tracker offers no signal about ownership. The cost is a backlog that reads as instance work while being platform work: re-filing alone took one instance from 2 open issues to 0 and another from 9 to 5, with every remainder genuinely instance-level. Candidates: an issue template asking which path the symptom lives in, or a triage step that resolves the answer against core-manifest.json
fixesIn: not fixed — the check exists (core-manifest.json, longest-prefix-wins); nothing invokes it at filing time

summary: A requirement can be asserted from a pattern and turn out not to exist. #994 listed four prerequisites for the S3 upload, one of which was an s3:PutObject grant for the deploy role. That was inferred from how least-privilege estates usually work, not checked. The role in fact carries AdministratorAccess (attached imperatively by AwsAdapter.setupOidcTrust), so no IAM change was needed at all. Harmless here — the issue was over-specified, not under-specified — but the same habit in the other direction is how a missing grant reaches production, and the corpus already carries "S3 prefix not in IAM" as a real defect. An issue's prerequisite list is a claim about the world and deserves the same evidence standard as a finding
fixesIn: practice — check the privilege model before listing it as work

summary: Nothing exercises deploy-app.yml where it is written, and five defects accumulated in one step because of it. biffo-template owns the workflow and is non-deployable, so the file is authored in a repo that cannot run it and only ever executes in an instance. Defects therefore surface one per deploy attempt, each masking the next, at ~40 minutes per round trip (template PR → tag → npm → core upgrade → instance PR → deploy). Four of the five were shell and path errors reachable with no AWS at all — wrong ../ depth twice, a missing interpreter, a zip written and read at different paths. A smoke harness running the step's shell logic against a fixture tree, in the repo that owns it, would collapse that loop from five deploys to one local test. Guards now exist for three of the five shapes, which is strictly better and still reactive: each was written *after* its defect shipped
fixesIn: biffo-template — a packaging smoke harness; not started

summary: A guard that excludes a category for one good reason silently excludes it for all reasons. workflow-relative-paths.test.ts exempted build artifacts from its existence check because they legitimately do not exist at checkout — correct, and its own comment argues it well. Nothing said what *was* still checkable about them, so the exemption became total and bug 4 lived in it for as long as the file has existed. The recovered assertion (agreement: what a step's zip writes is what its fileb:// must read) needs no filesystem and no knowledge of the artifact. Worth asking of every exclusion already in the estate's guards: *what remains true about the thing you just stopped checking?*
fixesIn: biffo-template — pattern, not a single fix

summary: botocore is bundled into every Lambda package and is already in the runtime. Measuring tabsii-platform's package during the size incident: 184MB unzipped, of which botocore ~24MB is shipped despite AWS providing it. It is not the largest item (numpy + numpy.libs at 57MB, via shapely, is), but it is the only one that is pure waste rather than a real dependency. Not enough on its own to clear the inline cap (~68MB base64 after removal, still over), which is why it was not pursued under time pressure — but it is free size in every instance, forever, and nothing measures package composition at all
fixesIn: not fixed — exclude boto3/botocore from the package; revisit alongside the S3 artifacts bucket

summary: Relaxing strict removes the guard against exactly this. H3 turned strict off on biffo-template on 2026-07-28 to end the rebase race. A side effect nobody costed: a branch no longer has to be up to date before merging, so a stale whole-file rewrite is now *more* likely to land silently. The experiment's falsification criteria measure merge friction and say nothing about content loss
fixesIn: H3 review 2026-08-11 — add content loss to what the experiment watches

summary: The portal serves 404s as HTTP 200, so a dead URL is indistinguishable from a live one. A reported failure at /dashboard/new-idea-scout/ was investigated as an application bug; the path renders Next.js's *"This page could not be found"* with a 200 status (static-export behaviour), and no dashboard route exists in either the instance's or the template's portal source. The real app is at /idea-scout/. Cost the first minutes of a live incident chasing a page that does not exist, and it means no monitor or link-checker can detect a broken portal link

RECURRENCE, and the fix was half-applied: the same root-marker defect was fixed for JavaScript and left in place for Python. tabsii-crm ran one check in eight on a ~700-line TS+Python change and printed verify passed; the only thing that executed was terraform-fmt. Two distinct causes, and the second is the interesting one. (1) The js_dirs() fix existed upstream but had never reached the siblings — biffo core upgrade reaches *instances* only, and nothing carried it to repos with neither biffo.core.json nor a manifest. (2) The Python block was still if [ -f pyproject.toml ] at the root, with no py_dirs() equivalent, so even a freshly-scaffolded sibling skipped ruff, format and pyright entirely. The original row's own rationale — *"every plugin, every sibling, both runner repos"* — applies verbatim to Python and was fixed for one language only. Condition: a fix written against one instance of a general defect gets scoped to that instance, and the generalisation in its own justification is not re-read when it lands
fixesIn: biffo-template — py_dirs() + scripts/shared-sync.sh for the distribution channel

summary: A security gate was excluded from the pre-push gate on a rationale that was factually wrong, and the exclusion list is hand-written prose nothing checks. verify-parity.test.ts excluded Bandit with *"writes a report artefact CI uploads; the finding gate is the upload step, not the run"*. bandit -ll exits 1 on findings, and it is the run step that fails — CI proved it on tabsii-platform#313 (SAST (Bandit) → ##[error]Process completed with exit code 1) after verify passed locally. The parity test does its job: it forces every CI check to be either present or explicitly excluded. What nothing checks is whether the stated reason for an exclusion is true, and a wrong reason reads exactly like a considered one. Bandit runs in ~2s, offline, over the working tree — it met every inclusion criterion the script states for itself

Three Cognito client IDs in one origin's localStorage; two belong to destroyed pools. AWS has exactly one pool and one client — pure browser residue, but any code picking the "first" match grabs a dead token

RunOutcome.trigger_payload unwrapped trigger_event['payload'] and fell back to {}. Nothing in the system writes that envelope — dispatch_event stores the event flat and the engine reads it flat — so the property returned {} for EVERY real run since the seam shipped. The module docstring's worked example taught the broken call, eleven lines below a sentence describing trigger_event as 'the whole triggering payload'

An SESv2 configuration set was created with a bounce/complaint event destination, but never attached to the identity mail is actually sent as. Bounces reached account-level AWS/SES metrics (which need no configuration set) while the SNS destination saw nothing, so the consumer Lambda had no CloudWatch log group at all — it had never once been invoked. The feature shipped, was green, and was inert

SES publishes two different envelopes. A configuration-set event destination names the type 'eventType' and spells the rendering failure 'RenderingFailure'; a classic identity notification topic names it 'notificationType' and spells it 'Rendering Failure'. The handler read notificationType only, so its first ever real invocation resolved to None and dropped the bounce it existed to handle. Same assumed-payload-shape class as the row above it, in the same feature, four hours apart

RECURRENCE of 'an admin panel rendered a 500 as No catalog entries yet' in a different repo. A lead's Activity timeline inferred 'Nothing sent or logged yet.' from an empty array, and the array is empty in three situations — request in flight, genuinely empty, and request FAILED, because .catch(() => undefined) swallowed the error into the same []. A 403 or 500 therefore told the reader a candidate had never been contacted. The earlier instance was logged 'unfiled' and the pattern was not generalised, so it recurred

Merging the core upgrade that ships tracked .githooks/ does NOT arm them. core.hooksPath is per-clone config set by package.json's prepare, so an existing clone keeps pointing at the old generated dir until someone runs pnpm install once. The merge reads as done while the guard stays inert — the same shape as the defect it fixes. Verified empirically: a fresh worktree off the merged dev still reported hooksPath=.husky/_ with .husky/_ absent

Issue #374 described the worktree-hooks gap IN ITS OWN BODY — 'hooks do not run in a fresh clone... easy to hit when working in a throwaway clone or a worktree' — called it 'arguably the larger issue', proposed two fixes, then shipped only the pre-push hook and closed. The named-but-unfixed half cost 1h43m five days later. A closed issue is not evidence its stated findings were addressed

core.hooksPath was `.husky/_` -- a RELATIVE path git resolves against each worktree's root, pointing at a GITIGNORED directory created only by `prepare: husky` on `pnpm install`. AGENTS.md section 1 mandates a fresh worktree per unit of work, so the required workflow disarmed its own gates: git skipped every hook with no warning, no error and no output. 7 of 37 working trees armed. Verified on tabsii-platform/.worktrees/discovery-rls -- three tracked hook files, no .husky/_, therefore no pyright, no lint-staged and no commitlint on anything committed there

The local gate checked the repo ROOT only. In the ten repos with no root package.json or pyproject.toml -- every sibling, every plugin -- it printed `n/a - no package.json in this repo` and then `verify passed`, on repos whose entire frontend is TypeScript and whose API is Python. tabsii-crm ran ONE check (terraform-fmt) on a 700-line TypeScript-and-Python change and reported a pass. Worse than the missing hooks it was built to fix: a repo with no hooks makes no claim, this one claimed to have checked

The parity guard that compares the local gate to CI ran ONLY in biffo-template -- the single repo with both a root package.json and a root pyproject.toml, i.e. the one place the root-only assumption held. It validated the gate where the gate was already correct, and could not have caught the blind spot in any of the ten repos that had it. A guard scoped to the environment it was written in is not a guard

Sibling and plugin repos are separate repositories with no core-manifest.json, so `biffo core upgrade` cannot reach them. The documented channel was 'vendor into the skeleton, plus a one-time manual copy-in for existing ones' -- which only ever helps repos created afterwards, and nothing prompts the copy-in. Second occurrence of the same absence: it is how AGENTS.md drifted 68 lines behind in tabsii (#559), and how eight repos ended up two gate versions stale

bandit was excluded from the local gate with the rationale 'writes a report artefact CI uploads; the finding gate is the upload step, not the run'. False: `bandit -ll` exits non-zero on findings and it is the RUN step that fails -- tabsii-platform PR #313 job 90502765804, SAST (Bandit), exit code 1, on a change whose local verify had passed. The exclusion was written from INTENT and never checked against a real run, and it stood for a fortnight

The local gate ran a FIXED check list tuned against biffo-template, so it was repeatedly STRICTER than the repo's CI: terraform-fmt over infra/ where CI checks only modules/; bandit over -r services where CI scans only template-owned paths (three B310s in user-owned services/idea-scout/, a push CI would have passed); bandit at all in plugin repos whose CI has no bandit step and where the tool is not installed. Patched three times before the cause was fixed. A gate stricter than CI blocks correct work and drives BIFFO_SKIP_VERIFY -- the counter-metric H4 pre-registered as refuting itself

The shared-file drift detector compared the template against each LOCAL WORKING COPY, so twelve repos that were entirely current reported DRIFTED immediately after their sync PRs merged -- the clones had simply not been pulled. Resolving the branch through origin/HEAD then reported three more as missing everything, because it points at `main` in several clones and main is a stale release branch. A drift detector that fires on a stale checkout is one you learn to ignore

The shared-sync tool reported 'PUSH REFUSED (run the gate there and look)' for every push failure. The first real cause was a plain non-fast-forward against a previous run's branch, and the gate was GREEN in that repo -- the diagnostic sent you to read a passing log. Same class as the defects the tool distributes a gate to prevent, committed by the distributor

verify.sh ran `pytest -q --no-cov`. --no-cov is a pytest-cov FLAG, and repos without that plugin -- biffo-plugin-ideation, whose CI runs plain `uv run pytest -q` -- reject it with `unrecognized arguments`, so the gate refused a push CI would have passed. H5 pre-registered the recurrence of 'gate stricter than CI' as a condition that REFUTES H5, and it recurred within hours of that page being written. Caught during estate rollout, in the first repo whose pytest setup differed from the ones it was written against

`verify.sh --list` skipped the pytest timing probe entirely, so the tool disagreed with itself: tabsii-crm ran `OK pytest(services/api) 2s` while --list reported pytest absent, and gate-coverage.sh reads --list. Fixing it forced an explicit choice of guess direction with no cached measurement: guessing 'fast' makes --list CLAIM a check the gate may not run (fail-open); guessing 'slow' under-reports one it does (visible, self-correcting once the first real run writes the measurement). Both were tried in that order

pytest was excluded from the local gate by a blanket rule with a manual opt-in nobody ever issued. Measured: 51.2s in biffo-template, 57.4s biffo-platform, 85.6s tabsii-platform -- but 1.7s tabsii-marketplace, 2.1s tabsii-geo, 2.5s tabsii-intake, 2.7s tabsii-crm. The exclusion was correct for the three repos it was written against and wrong for the four it was applied to, so THE FASTEST SUITES IN THE ESTATE WERE THE ONES NOT BEING RUN. An exclusion written against one repo class and applied to all of them

Two findings were nearly reported from tool output that was itself wrong. A conventional-commit audit measured 12% violations in tabsii-platform using a regex that rejected `feat(db,api):` -- commas are legal in a scope, so the tool was wrong and the repo was fine. Separately, `biffo.sh check release-subject` printed 'No base ref' and looked like a fail-open until its exit code was read properly: it exits 2, loudly. Both would have produced a scoreboard row asserting a defect that does not exist

A cadence step could not be created AT ALL: crm_cadence_steps.brand_id is NOT NULL (denormalised for RLS) and the sibling never supplied it. Every test for the feature constructed a CadenceStep OBJECT — and a Python constructor makes you pass brand_id, so all of them did. Nothing exercised the HTTP path, which is the only place the omission exists. Unit suites green on both sides of the boundary; the feature could not create a step

Every compiled cadence email step FAILED AT DISPATCH: the email action declares `from` required with no default, and the step builder hardcoded to/subject/body without it. Invisible everywhere before a real send — the compile reports success, the definition looks correct in the database, and the failure exists only inside the orchestrator past EventBridge. Only a live capture surfaced it

A merged PR ASSERTED a verification nobody performed. #323 built POST /leads/{id}/status and its description said 'the CRM is pointed here'. It was not — the drawer still sent status through the generic PUT, so the fix existed in Core and nothing in the product used it, and #320 was closed while the failure it described still happened. Caught only by checking which endpoint the deployed UI actually calls before testing

RLS hardening blocked the write path it was designed to permit. Module 052 gave lead_cadence_enrolments a SELECT policy and no others so a caller could not desynchronise it from its scheduled runs; RLS applies to the ENDPOINT's session too, so the transition matched zero rows and converting a lead 500'd with StaleDataError — leaving the cadence armed. The logic was tested thoroughly on SQLite, WHICH HAS NO POLICIES, so every one of those tests ran against a session that could write anything

A deploy-watcher matched 'the newest run named Deploy' without pinning the commit SHA, and reported success for the PREVIOUS commit's deploy — the new one had not been created yet, by one second. Nearly produced a fabricated defect report ('the fix does not work on dev') from a green signal about the wrong artifact. Earlier watchers in the same session DID pin the SHA; the inconsistency was the bug

An approved implementation plan specified a mechanism that CANNOT work: cadence steps were to trigger on lead.captured with a synthetic cadence_id in trigger_filter, but trigger_filter is an exact match over the event payload and lead.captured carries no cadence_id. Every compiled step would have been silently inert; dropping the filter instead makes two active cadences both fire for one lead. Caught by reading _matches_trigger_filter BEFORE building, not after

Resolving an append-only corpus conflict with a regex that assumed BOTH sides had content: this conflict had an EMPTY HEAD side, so the resolver matched nothing and printed '0 conflicts resolved', which was read as 'no conflicts'. Raw conflict markers were committed and pushed into evidence.jsonl. The JSON validation in the same command DID catch it -- and the push ran anyway, because it was chained on the same shell line rather than gated on the validation's exit status. A check that reports without blocking, against the corpus that records that exact failure class

scripts/protection-audit.sh, written specifically to catch a permanently-skipped security gate, was itself fail-open on its first run. It read only stdout and matched with `case`; `gh api` prints its 404 body TO STDOUT for an unprotected branch, so three genuinely unprotected branches fell through to the wildcard and were reported `ok ... {"message":"Branch not protected"} required checks`, exit 0. Found by reading every line of the output rather than the summary

Issue #643 family 5 asked the template to 'make the app DB role name a variable'. It ALREADY WAS -- var.app_db_user existed at core-v0.127.0, added before the issue was filed -- and the second half (make the secret RESOURCE name a variable) is impossible: HCL resource labels are not interpolatable. Both sides already set an identical name, so only the Terraform state address differs and a `moved` block resolves it with no destroy, contradicting the instance's claim that adopting would recreate a live credential. An issue's premise going stale between filing and scheduling, on a claim nobody re-checked

The deployed Core Lambda package contains 1,643 .py files and ZERO .pyc, and /var/task is read-only so the bytecode cache can never be written. deploy-app.yml deletes __pycache__ deliberately, as 'build-time dead weight', to fit an upload size cap. Precompiling takes import 4105ms -> 1575ms at calibrated CPU: a build step added for a size limit silently became ~60% of every cold start, and set the floor under every timeout in the estate. No gate could see it because the artifact was never profiled -- only the source was

Issue #695 asserts build_core_crud_router() returns zero routes on a second call because 'the first call consumes the registry'. Could not be reproduced from two independent directions: the agent writing the #668 guard called it three times against an opted-in model and got identical non-empty sets, and four attempts here returned the SAME count on calls 1/2/3 (never populated-then-empty), with a validation warning firing identically on all three -- which alone disproves consumption. The likely real cause is that app.routes is not flat on FastAPI 0.138: include_router leaves an _IncludedRouter placeholder with no .path, so the idiom the issue quotes reads zero usable routes without anything being consumed. A property of the reader, not the function

The 'Where the work actually lands' table -- headed 'Generated, not typed' and explicitly warning that hand-typed counts go stale -- was itself stale by a factor of 2.5: it read 99 corpus rows and 68 for biffo-template while the corpus held 248 and 126. Three sessions rewrote it in one day (200 -> 99 -> 248) because the figures are transcribed by hand from a generated report, and concurrent sessions cannot converge on a hand-copied number. A generator emitting the markdown directly does not exist

RECURRENCE, third instance in one session, and the class is 'the instrument was the defect'. integrationHealth.redMinutes measured failure-to-recovery wall-clock, so a branch left red at 11:47 and green at 06:36 next morning scored 21.1h -- 89% of it overnight with ZERO pushes against it. Nobody was blocked; everyone was asleep. That number ranked FIRST of five findings on the standup's first real run, and metrics.md instructed the reader to MULTIPLY it by concurrency. The genuinely blocked window was 2.3h, which ranks the finding last. The estate had already established the distinction one metric over, for the runner fleet -- 'flat queue under an idle fleet is not contention' -- and never applied it here

RECURRENCE of 'suspect the ruler', and I was the one who did it: I diagnosed an exit-status bug in practices-daily.sh from a theory, asserted it twice as fact, and built a worktree to fix it. There was no bug. The 'exit 1' came from my own `| head -22`, which SIGPIPEs the script and makes PIPESTATUS[0] report 141; the proposed mechanism was wrong too, since a trailing `if` with a false condition exits 0 in bash. Cost was not the wrong theory but the confidence: it was repeated in two summaries before anyone ran the script without a pipe. The honest residue was real -- the log had no terminal marker, so a truncated run and a complete one were indistinguishable, which is what made the misreading possible

The tool built to find fail-open shipped one, and failed its own test within six minutes of merging. practices-standup.mjs read docs/practices/data/ from wherever it ran; the primary checkout carries only what was merged to dev, and today's snapshot lives on chore/practices-snapshots which is deliberately never merged. Run with default arguments it printed a confident, fully formatted ranking of a TWO-DAY-OLD snapshot with no warning. Worse here than in most places: the output's whole purpose is to direct a day's effort, so it does not merely fail to help, it spends the budget on an old problem and reports success

The 04:30 practices cron 401'd on all fifteen repos and still wrote a well-formed 9.5KB snapshot -- every repo `unmeasured`, estate.merges 0 -- then stopped before rendering, so the bookmarked dashboard silently served the previous day. gh stores its token in the GNOME keyring and hosts.yml carries no oauth_token, so cron has no session D-Bus to read it through. Same class as the ssh-agent gap the script already compensated for twenty lines above: a credential that exists only inside a desktop session. Graceful degradation was right for one unreadable repo and wrong for all of them -- 'nothing could be measured' is not an observation, it is a broken job

One unbatched distribution produced 35% of a day's merges and no metric could see it. 81 of 226 merges on 2026-07-29 were `chore(shared): sync template-shared files` -- ~7 rounds across 12 repos, 6 of the 7 touching scripts/verify.sh, i.e. one gate iterated upstream and redistributed after every iteration instead of once when it settled. It inflated toilRatio to 57.4% against 32% recorded, inverted the platform/product split to 54.5% product, and drove small-repo repushRate to 66-77%. Every existing metric is a share or a rate, and amplification is invisible to both: it looks exactly like a busy day. Priced in runner minutes it is only ~6.8h and ranks FIFTH, so share of merges is not cost -- the manual read that called it the biggest item was wrong and the tool was right
fixesIn: not fixed -- summariseAmplification measures it; batching the distribution is the open change

summary: PREVENTED, not fixed, and the best row of the day: a coherent, well-written issue whose stated mechanism would have shipped a lying endpoint. #648 items 2+3 ask for /health to report the deployed core version by bundling repo-root `core.version` and walking up to find it. Measured on biffo-platform: biffo.core.json = 0.181.0, core.version = 0.41.17 -- so /health would have reported a version 140 releases behind, in the one endpoint whose entire job is saying what is deployed. That is #788 rebuilt deliberately. It also self-destructs: #842, merged four hours earlier the same day, now DELETES a core.version below the authority, so the feature would read the wrong version until the next upgrade and nothing after. The issue was written against the pre-#423 world and nothing re-checked its premise. Goal is still valid; the mechanism had to change to biffo.core.json or a deploy-time env var
fixesIn: not built -- correction recorded on the issue, mechanism now a decision

summary: A repair tool would have silently reverted a running experiment. branch-protection-apply.ts hard-coded `strict: true` calling it 'not negotiable', while H3 has strict:false on biffo-template's dev deliberately until 2026-08-11. The audit reports that as a not-strict finding -- correctly -- and --fix fires on ANY finding, so `biffo check branch-protection --fix` would have applied strict:true and undone the experiment with no message saying so. The only trace would have been H3's counter-metrics quietly changing shape, i.e. the experiment would have reported a result about a condition that was no longer in force. Two tools in the same repo disagreeing about policy, with one able to overwrite the other
fixesIn: biffo-template (absence of protection = gap, present-but-relaxed = decision)

summary: RECURRENCE, fourth and fifth instances in one day, and the shape now has a name: THE CHECK EXISTS AND DOES NOT CHECK. #694's guard existed and passed -- its scope was narrower than its subject, asserting over Core's module constants while the UI reads registered_events(). #697's test was literally named 'names the 404-means-403 trap' and fed it an ENEEDAUTH log, so it asserted the PROSE mentioned 404 while the classifier had no E404 entry at all and a real E404 collected 're-dispatch this workflow' -- the loop the same code documents, at one burned version number per attempt. #764's migration guard was correct only because Alembic happens not to inherit db_search_path, which nothing stated or tested. summary: A guard exempted build artifacts from its EXISTENCE check -- correctly -- and thereby exempted them from EVERY check, which is where the next bug lived. workflow-relative-paths.test.ts asserts that a workflow step executing a script by relative path points at a script that exists. Its own comment records a deliberate narrowing: `../lambda.zip` and `../plugin-host.zip` are runtime artifacts, legitimately absent from the checkout, and a guard that cries wolf on correct code gets deleted. Both halves of that reasoning are right. The unexamined step was treating "cannot check existence" as "cannot check anything": the core API step wrote its zip to the step directory and read it back one level higher, and no assertion covered it. A runtime artifact cannot be checked for existence but CAN be checked for agreement -- what a step zip writes is what its fileb:// must read -- which needs no filesystem. Interpolated names stop needing an exemption under that rule too, since <dir>/../<name>.zip normalises to <name>.zip whatever <dir> expands to. The generalisable trap: when a guard excludes a category for one good reason, state what still IS checkable about that category, or the exclusion silently becomes total

summary: A size guard turned a capacity ceiling into an outage by failing rather than degrading. Bytecode precompilation (#724) adds ~56% to the Lambda zip and buys ~60% of a ~4.0s cold-start init, because /var/task is read-only so every cold start recompiles ~1,620 files. tabsii-platform outgrew the inline request cap at 60.3MB zipped / ~80.2MB base64 against ~70MB, and the guard exited 1 -- correct about the cap, wrong about the consequence, because bytecode is an OPTIMISATION and the deployed code is byte-for-byte identical without it. The instance therefore could not deploy at all rather than deploying slightly slower, and its /health sat 173 releases behind. Measured composition: 184MB unzipped, numpy+numpy.libs 57MB via shapely, botocore 24MB (already present in the Lambda runtime and therefore pure waste), pillow 20MB via reportlab. The fix degrades -- drop __pycache__, re-zip, warn loudly -- and fails only if still over without bytecode, at which point nothing else would save it. Stopgap by construction: the real fix is an S3-based update (250MB unzipped ceiling), blocked on an artifacts bucket that does not exist, because the only candidate bucket is CloudFront-served and shipping zips there would publish application source
fixesIn: biffo-template .github/workflows/deploy-app.yml -- degrade before fail; S3 artifacts bucket still outstanding

The declared scope becomes silently the opposite of the granted one, and whoami reports the role's intended shape either way. Closed by a trigger rather than the obvious composite FK: MATCH SIMPLE skips enforcement entirely when any referencing column is NULL, so the declarative spelling would have been a fail-open in the guard itself — the exact class it was written to close — and closing THAT hole needs a NOT NULL that rejects existing rows. It surfaced only because an unrelated metric disagreed with a setting: staleMergeShare counted merges that were not up to date on three repos carrying strict: true, which that gate makes impossible by construction. summary: A scaffold-time exception with no expiry becomes the permanent state, and the fix is to give it a lifetime rather than delete it. `biffo init` sets enforce_admins:false so that a RESUMED, step-checkpointed run can still commit to branches an earlier attempt already protected -- a correct reason, correctly scoped to the duration of the scaffold. Nothing ever closed it, so every repo the CLI ever made was born advisory and stayed that way: 26 of 27 estate branches (#1052). The wrong fix is flipping the literal, which breaks resumability; the right one is a sealing step whose position IS the safety property -- last, after every git-object write -- so a run interrupted before it leaves branches writable and a run that reached it has nothing left to write. That made the invariant testable without creating real repos: assert CALL ORDER (commitFiles/fastForwardBranch always precede the seal) rather than the step list's shape, and the guard was then proved by moving the seal before the git write and watching it fire, not merely by deleting the seal and watching it fail. Deleting-and-failing only proves the test notices absence; the defect it must actually catch is misplacement. Also: the legacy `github_config` checkpoint deliberately does NOT alias the new step, because a session written before it has genuinely not sealed -- aliasing would have resumed every existing session into the old state silently, which is the original bug wearing the fix's clothes.
