fixesIn: biffo-template (#1063, #1068) — rebuilt upstream, instance branch deleted

summary: An ADR accepted the day before asserted a safety property that had never been implemented, twice, in the section describing that safety property. ADR-0100 stated parseSearch "already refuses to hydrate a node above the caller's ceiling". It computed a ceiling and never consulted it. Because a Unit Owner holds brands.read by ancestor grant, their ancestor brand *is* in the array the check trusted, so ?brand=<id> would have been honoured — the exact traversal the ADR said was already prevented. An ADR is read as a statement of what holds; this one shipped a belief
fixesIn: tabsii-platform#466 — corrected in place with a dated note; refusal written and tested in tabsii-crm#166

summary: A required behaviour was dropped in the hand-off from plan to subagent prompt, and six milestones of green CI never noticed — it was found by opening the page. ADR-0100 decided /login should forward an already-authenticated visitor; the plan's milestone said so; the prompt written from that milestone omitted it. Nothing downstream could catch it: there was no test for a feature nobody had been asked to build. The whole verification apparatus of this session — unit tests, fail-first proofs, CI, deploy checks — was blind to a *missing requirement*, which only a human route exercised
surfacedIn: biffo-template — found on deployed dev by loading /login while signed in

summary: A CHECK constraint made its own feature impossible, and no test could have caught it because no test lane carries the constraint. Module 074 gave tabsii.lessons `CHECK (media_asset_id IS NOT NULL OR body_text IS NOT NULL)` -- 'a lesson has to render something'. Right intent, wrong moment: authoring is create-then-attach, because an upload needs a row to attach TO. So every POST /api/v1/lessons failed with CheckViolationError, and the constraint did not enforce the invariant, it made the invariant unreachable. M2, M3, M4 and M5 all shipped green through it. THE STRUCTURAL CAUSE: core's handler tests run on SQLite and the sibling's BFF tests run on fakes, and NEITHER carries the tabsii CHECK constraints, the RLS policies or the bucket CORS policy. The first real INSERT was a human clicking 'Add lesson' on dev -- the first time the constraint had ever been evaluated in its life. Fixed by dropping it: 'renders something' is a property of a lesson a LEARNER can reach, and learners only reach published courses, so it belongs at the publish transition, not on every INSERT.
surfacedIn: clicking the LMS authoring surface on dev; invisible to both test lanes
fixesIn: tabsii-platform#472 -- DDL module 075, applied to dev

summary: One click-through of a CI-green feature produced five defects, none reachable by any test in either repo. Beyond the CHECK constraint above: the generic CRUD layer rendered the raw asyncpg exception text into the page, leaking driver, table and constraint names to any authenticated caller (#473); the evidence bucket's CORS allows POST/PUT but not GET, so material can be linked or played but never fetched in-page, which blocks the inline PDF viewer document lessons will need (#475); the brand id lives only in React state and the frontend is a static export, so every link into an editor hard-navigates and dead-ends on a UUID prompt (lms#2); and an expired token surfaces API Gateway's raw {"message":"Unauthorized"} even though a refresh token is in localStorage and the app already renews on page load -- it just never does so on a 401, so every session breaks at the one-hour mark mid-task (lms#3). Common shape: each is an interaction between two layers that no single layer's tests instantiate -- app and Postgres, app and S3 CORS, React and static-export navigation, client and API Gateway authorizer.
surfacedIn: LMS v1 M5 click-through on dev, after M1-M5 all merged CI-green

summary: Coordinate-based browser clicking manufactured a phantom defect, and it took three attempts to notice the instrument rather than the subject. Driving the LMS authoring UI, two 'Add learning path' clicks appeared to fail silently -- input cleared, no error, nothing created, and the API confirmed zero rows. The conclusion forming was 'the create fails silently', which would have been filed against working code. The cause was that the page re-lays-out between the screenshot and the click, so coordinates captured from a screenshot are already stale when used; both clicks landed on empty space. Clicking by element ref instead worked first time. The general rule: a UI automation failure is evidence about EITHER the app or the harness, and the harness is the one whose state went stale a second ago. Before filing a UI defect found by coordinate clicking, re-run it by reference -- it costs one call and is the difference between a finding and a fabrication. This is biffo-verify's 'suspect the ruler first' applied to a browser rather than a metric.
fixesIn: practice -- prefer ref-based clicking; re-run by ref before filing

summary: A scoped role's already-granted permission was dead on arrival for any query joining through it, and the RLS satisfiability guard caught the exact instance it was built for. Fixing tabsii-platform's onboarding dashboard needed a kpi_values -> kpi_definitions join (to scope a stalled-flag reading by brand+code) under a real Unit Owner session. Unit Owner already held kpi_values.read — genuinely usable standalone, since that table's RLS policy passes unit_id — but granting kpi_definitions.read alongside it still wasn't enough: kpi_definitions is brand-scoped with no unit_id column, so a unit-scoped role assignment can never match its policy directly, only an ancestor-visibility carve-out (module 024, previously covering only brands.read/regions.read) can satisfy it. test_rls_grant_satisfiability_pg.py's test_no_new_unsatisfiable_scoped_grants failed on the first CI push, correctly, on a permission code the guard's own author had never anticipated when writing it — and the same push also revealed a second, pre-existing, unrelated instance of the identical shape already sitting in KNOWN_UNSATISFIABLE (Regional HQ's kpi_definitions.read/region grant, unsatisfiable since the day it was first granted, via the broad %.read provisioning rule)
fixesIn: tabsii-platform #476 — fn_authorized ancestor-visibility extended to kpi_definitions.read (module 076), guard's ANCESTOR_READABLE/KNOWN_UNSATISFIABLE updated to match

summary: A repo's real TypeScript/CSS convention (single-quote, no semicolons) is enforced by nobody — not ESLint, not a .prettierrc, not CI — so it exists only as an unwritten habit every file happens to follow. Neither tabsii-platform's nor tabsii-crm's frontend carries a .prettierrc; prettier --write therefore falls back to its own defaults (double quotes, semicolons), which is the *opposite* of the house style every existing file demonstrates. Running it on a single changed file — a completely ordinary "let me format this" reflex — whole-file-reformatted every unrelated line in globals.css (3000+ lines) to the wrong style, twice in one session, once each in two different repos. Caught both times only by reading the diff before pushing, never by any tool. The gap: nothing stops the *next* agent from doing the same thing and not catching it, since the failure mode produces a large, plausible-looking, green diff
fixesIn: not fixed — candidates: commit a .prettierrc matching the actual house style so the tool's defaults stop disagreeing with the codebase, or add a format:check step that would catch a whole-file reformat before push

summary: A third-party API tightened a limit overnight and took the entire measurement programme dark in one step, with a guard that named the wrong cause. GitHub cut the GraphQL node budget server-side; 'gh pr list --json commits' expands to commits(first:100){nodes{authors(first:100)}}, so against a 100-PR page it asks for 100x100x100 = 1,000,000 possible nodes against a 500,000 ceiling. The estimate is computed from the PAGE SIZE, not from what a repo holds, so lowering --limit does not help - 1000/500/250/100 all fail identically - and all 15 repos failed at once. Nothing local changed: gh 2.96.0 was a month old and the same query minus 'commits' still succeeded. The preflight guard (#917) worked exactly as designed and refused to write a hollow snapshot, but its diagnostic asserted 'the most likely cause is credentials: gh stores its token in the keyring' UNCONDITIONALLY - true of the 401 that motivated it, false here, and it sends the reader after a working keyring. So the day had no data at all, and the previous day's standup choice could not be closed: an outage in the measurement layer costs the ritual that depends on it, not just the numbers. Two lessons: a metric pipeline resting on an external API's implicit limits will break on someone else's schedule, and a guard that prints one hardcoded cause is not a diagnosis - a confidently wrong one costs more than none, because the reader spends the time disproving it.
surfacedIn: biffo-template daily practices cron (04:30 2026-08-02) - all 15 repos, FATAL, no snapshot written
fixesIn: fixed (#1086) - 'commits' fetched per-PR (1x100x100 = 10,000 nodes, inside budget) only for upgrade PRs whose body lacks the marker, since parseCarriedPrs reads the body first and the sole call site is already gated on isUpgradePr. Measured cost rather than assumed it: 107 extra requests across 1242 PRs over 90 days (8.6%), 0 of 743 on biffo-template. diagnoseTotalFetchFailure now names the node budget, credentials or a rate limit only when the error says so, and otherwise admits it does not know.

summary: A REQUIRED CI check had no local counterpart at all, and nothing said so. tabsii-platform's rls-test lane (real Postgres, RLS policies) was 9 of 13 locally-catchable failing CI steps across the estate in 24h - every one a genuine assertion failure on a feature branch, plus one re-runnability failure from leaked state, all of which a local run catches. scripts/verify.sh contained NO reference to Postgres in any form, so the gate printed 'verify passed' having never looked at a check that costs a ~7-minute round trip to discover. Locally the whole lane is ~2s to build the schema (alembic 0.74s + 85 DDL modules 1.3s) and ~28s for 310 tests. The general lesson is not 'add this check': it is that a gate claiming to mirror CI must be measured against CI's ACTUAL required checks, because a lane living in its own workflow file is invisible to a gate assembled from what the repo obviously has. Second-order: the fix must distinguish 'this repo does not have the thing' from 'this repo HAS it and the gate is blind to it' - printing both as a quiet n/a is how a gap gets read as coverage.
surfacedIn: estate-wide, concentrated in tabsii-platform (found ranking the 2026-08-02 standup)
fixesIn: fixed upstream (biffo-template#1089): a pg-test check selecting by the same test_*_pg.py CONVENTION the CI lane uses, three distinct states (quiet n/a / loud WARN + 'APPLICABLE BUT NOT RUN' / runs), and CI's own anti-fail-open assertions so a schema-less database FAILS rather than reporting 0-passed as success. Verified against the real repo: 310 tests pass in 33s through the gate, and it fails against an empty DB. Local DB helper still owed by tabsii-platform#487 - until then the gate warns rather than runs there.

summary: An alerting path that existed, read as coverage, and had never once fired. All three notify-send calls in practices-daily.sh were guarded on a non-empty DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS - correct-looking, and under cron always false, because the crontab exports PATH and nothing else so a cron child has no session bus. The daily job is the ONLY schedule that matters for these alerts, so the estate-audit notification had been a no-op since it was written. It surfaced because the 2026-08-02 collector outage was found by a human happening to run the standup, 40 minutes after a job that had already detected the problem and correctly refused to write bad data. The class: a guard written for the interactive case, applied to an automated one, where the condition it tests is structurally unsatisfiable - and nothing distinguishes 'did not need to notify' from 'could not notify'. Corollary worth keeping: the reliable surface is the artefact people already look at (here the bookmarked dashboard), not a channel that has to be checked.
surfacedIn: biffo-template scripts/practices-daily.sh, all three notify-send call sites
fixesIn: fixed (biffo-template#1090): _notify reconstructs the bus address from systemd's /run/user/<uid>/bus rather than inheriting it, still fully guarded so a failed notify cannot fail the job; plus an idempotent stale banner stamped onto the bookmarked dashboard on abort, which does not blank the last good data. Two defects caught while writing the tests: the first pass left the nudge call still guarded, and the regression assertion matched the comment DOCUMENTING the old guard rather than the guard itself (#957's substring-guard shape).

summary: Two guards for one authorization concept drifted, and the test written to prevent exactly that drift could not see it. tabsii's ADR-0010 makes permission_code authoritative and *superseding*, with a platform super-role short-circuit. require_crud_permission implemented that; require_principal_crud_permission was written to the template's semantics — the two axes ANDed, no admin bypass — so the same caller got different answers depending on which transport they arrived by. test_crud_permission_code.py's own docstring asserts "both transports honour the same axis", but its single principal-transport test uses a rule with a code and no required_role — a case the two semantics agree on. It was green throughout. The drift surfaced only when core 0.211.0 distributed an upstream test (test_crud_guard_agreement.py, keiranholloway/biffo-template#1019) that varies the inputs case-for-case and went red on arrival. Reachability mattered and was checked rather than assumed: the both-axes disagreement is currently unbuildable, but the platform-admin one needed only the endpoint control plane doing the single thing it exists for — putting a required_role on a plugin table — on the mount (/api/v1/internal/plugins/*) that external plugin traffic actually reaches. A test that asserts a property in prose and exercises only the agreeing cases is documentation, not a guard

An aws --query alias renamed a field to its own opposite, and the false reading was published to the user and written into durable memory before another session caught it. --query '{sandbox:ProductionAccessEnabled,...}' returned "sandbox": false, which reads naturally as *"sandbox: false, so we are out of the sandbox"*. It means ProductionAccessEnabled: false — SES production access is off. The disconfirming value was in the same response the whole time (SendQuota.Max24HourSend: 200.0, the sandbox quota) and went unread because the aliased field had already answered the question. Cost is not the lookup — it is that a wrong fact propagated into a memory file and a status report, then took a second session to detect and a third correction to unwind. Naming is part of the measurement: an alias that inverts its source turns a correct API response into a wrong answer that no gate can catch
surfacedIn: my own diagnosis, tabsii SES status
fixesIn: diagnostic practice — select fields under their own names ({ProductionAccessEnabled:ProductionAccessEnabled}), never a name that could be read as the negation

summary: A plugin Lambda's log silence is indistinguishable from "nothing matched", and a second signal corroborated the wrong reading. Verifying a newly authored user.invited workflow, the orchestrator invocation logged Received event and returned in 612ms with no dispatch line — exactly what a workflow matching nothing looks like. A second observation appeared to confirm it: the event envelope's tenant_id is the tabsii tenant UUID while the definition's is default. Both readings were wrong. The plugin only forwards; Core does the matching, against the *service principal's* tenant. GET /api/v1/orchestration/runs showed the run succeeded with an SES message_id. A bug was one step from being filed against working code. Absence of a log line is not absence of the behaviour — find the component that owns the decision and read its record
fixesIn: diagnostic practice; the run record is authoritative and nothing points you to it

summary: A milestone's deliverable was a database row, and nothing in any repo recreates it. 0012 M8 ("invitations actually arrive") has two halves: an app_login_url repoint that shipped as a normal PR, and the user.invited → email workflow, which is a row in dev's database — because that is what a workflow definition *is* under ADR-0010, live data managed from the product rather than config-as-code. The consequence is silent and total: a fresh staging, prod, or rebuilt dev has the invite path sending nothing, with no migration, no seed, and no test that fails. The milestone reads as complete in every artifact a reviewer would check. Deliberately not "fixed" by adding a seed: a seeding mechanism would become a second authority competing with the product surface, which is the tension worth deciding rather than papering over
fixesIn: undecided — either a documented environment-standup step, or an ADR-0010 seeding path

summary: A blocker was recorded as a skills failure on a premise nobody checked, and the recorded lesson argued for building the wrong thing. A React-controlled portal form discards programmatically-set input — true, and a real browser-automation limit. It was written up as "the second React-controlled form this session with no API alternative", which turned a UI limitation into an argument for investing in browser tooling. The second half was never checked and was false: routers/orchestration.py exposes the full REST surface the form wraps (list/create/get/update/enabled/delete), and creating the workflow through it took one curl. A wrong premise recorded as a lesson is worse than no lesson — it outlives the session and directs future investment
fixesIn: diagnostic practice — before recording a UI as the only route, grep the routers for the resource

summary: A milestone can be "done" with half of it living only in a database, and every artifact a reviewer checks still reads complete. 0012 M8's app_login_url repoint is a PR; its user.invited workflow is a row, because ADR-0010 deliberately makes workflow definitions live data rather than config-as-code. Both halves are correct. But there is no migration, no seed, no fixture and no test tied to the second one, so a fresh staging, prod or rebuilt dev has the invite path silently sending nothing — and the PR, the CI run, the implementation doc and the issue all look finished. The obvious fix (seed the definition) is not obviously right: a seeding mechanism becomes a second authority competing with the product surface the ADR made authoritative, and then the two drift. The general shape is worth naming: any feature whose deliverable is data has no artifact for "did this land in environment X", and the estate has no convention for that at all. Candidates: a per-environment smoke check that asserts the *behaviour* (invite → run record) rather than the row, or an explicit environment-standup checklist that is allowed to be manual but must exist
fixesIn: undecided — the tension is the decision

summary: Nothing prices how far a wrong fact travels, so a sub-minute measurement error outranks a half-hour investigation and the page cannot show it. This session's cost note records both: ~35 min of deliberate RBAC investigation producing one durable correct answer, and one mis-aliased --query field producing a wrong answer that reached a user-facing report, a durable memory file, a second session's contradiction and a third correction. The scoreboard gives each one row. Every field it has — class, surfaced-in, fix-repo, status — describes the defect; none describes the blast radius of the belief. That matters more here than in most codebases, because facts get written into agent memory and are then quoted by later sessions as established, which is a propagation channel with no review step and no expiry. Candidates: a propagated-to field on rows where a wrong fact was published before being caught, or a rule that any fact written to durable memory from a single command's output must name the command and the exact field
fixesIn: not fixed — no mechanism proposed yet

summary: A local gate's own cached state can manufacture failures that look exactly like the developer's bug. Building the new local Postgres gate, a test database about an hour old -- built before two unrelated PRs merged -- produced 23 failures in a module nothing in the working tree had touched. Rebuilt from the same tree it passed 336/336, and passed 336 again on an immediate re-run, so the lane was genuinely re-runnable and every failure was the stale schema. The trap is that the first read of that result was WRONG in an instructive way: 23 failures on a second run against a reused database looks exactly like leaked test state, and that conclusion would have driven the wrong design (rebuild every time, or hunt a non-existent teardown bug). Only rebuilding and re-running twice distinguished them. Generalisation: any local gate holding cached state between runs -- a database, a container, a build cache, a fixture directory -- must treat freshness as a first-class property, because a stale artefact does not fail loudly, it fails as somebody else's code. And a gate that produces failures which are not the developer's fault is worse than no gate: it is the fastest route to the bypass that H4 pre-registered as refuting the whole local-gate programme.
surfacedIn: tabsii-platform pg lane, while building the local gate's database helper
fixesIn: fixed (biffo-template#1093): scripts/pg-test-db.sh fingerprints the migrations and DDL by CONTENT (mtime survives a branch switch; content does not), stores the fingerprint inside the database so it cannot outlive a drop, and rebuilds only on a mismatch - reuse 0.3s, rebuild 4s. It also refuses to record a fingerprint against a database holding under half the policies the DDL declares, because blessing a half-built schema makes the NEXT run trust it. Distribution to the repo that surfaced it is blocked on an unrelated core-upgrade conflict, tabsii-platform#491.

summary: A test that 'simulates' an environment by BLANKING a variable can activate the very fallback it meant to disable -- and the resulting side effect degraded a full working day. practices-daily-alert.test.ts set DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS='' to simulate cron, but an empty value is precisely the case _notify was written to handle, so it reconstructed the address from /run/user/<uid>/bus and called the REAL notify-send at -u critical, which never auto-expires in GNOME. Eight permanent desktop cards per `pnpm test` (2+3+2+1 across abortRuns). COST DERIVATION, because this is the most disruptive item of the day and should not be ranked by the fix alone: the alert test merged at 05:45Z (#1090) and the fix at 12:49Z (#1121), a 7h 04m window in which every test run planted eight cards; the effort log records 570 minutes of session work inside it (06:19, 06:20, 07:21, 08:14, 11:51), all of it interrupted, and the operator's own report was that it 'completely slowed me down'. 75 min of that is direct diagnosis and fix; ~60 min is a conservative attribution for interruption and lost focus across the window, and it is an estimate rather than a measurement. Two properties made it survive: the side effect was invisible to every gate (the suite was green, and a notification is not an assertion), and the card MISATTRIBUTED ITSELF -- it read 'Practices collection FAILED, the dashboard is stale', so the obvious diagnosis was a broken collector. The collector was healthy throughout: the log held exactly one real failure and the 05:53 run had succeeded, pushed and cleared the banner. Generalisation: a test inheriting process.env and PATH is NOT sandboxed, and any test that shells out can reach the developer's real session bus, desktop, keyring or network. Stub the binary on PATH rather than trying to disable it through configuration -- stubbing also turns an invisible side effect into an assertable one, which is what made the replace-don't-stack behaviour testable at all.
surfacedIn: keiranholloway/biffo-template cli/src/lib/practices-daily-alert.test.ts, reported by the operator as 'hundreds of notifications while working'
fixesIn: fixed (biffo-template#1121): tests stub notify-send on PATH and pass a non-empty bus address so nothing touches the real bus; _notify additionally replaces its card via --print-id/--replace-id instead of stacking, and honours PRACTICES_NO_DESKTOP_ALERT as an opt-OUT. Measured by the D-Bus notification id counter: 8 ids per run before, 0 after, 0 for a full `pnpm test`. Replacement then verified against the REAL GNOME daemon (same id reused) and under a real cron-like env -i (three failures, one card, id file at /tmp as designed).

summary: A log whose writer is EXTERNAL to the thing being logged cannot record every path, and reads as a complete history anyway. ~/.practices-daily.log is written by the crontab line's `>> logfile 2>&1` redirect, not by practices-daily.sh itself -- so it records cron runs and ONLY cron runs, and every interactive run, agent run and test-harness invocation of the same code is structurally invisible to it. Asked why hundreds of failure notifications were arriving, the log answered 'one failure, at 03:30'. That was true, and it was not an answer to the question. ~25 minutes went into a theory built on it (that dev/agent runs were tripping the EXIT trap) and a proposed `[ -t 1 ]` TTY guard which would have prevented NONE of the real events, because vitest runs with stdio 'pipe' and is not a TTY either -- a guard that would have read as protection while missing the measured cause. It was dropped before shipping only because the operator said the alerts were still arriving. The measurement that actually settled it -- read the D-Bus notification id counter, run the suite, read it again -- took under two minutes and was available from the first minute. Generalisation: before quoting a log as evidence of what did or did not happen, establish WHO WRITES IT and which invocation paths reach that writer. Absence of a log line is evidence about the logger's coverage first, and about the world second.
fixesIn: unfixed as a mechanism -- the redirect still lives in the crontab and nothing marks the log as cron-only. Recorded as a diagnostic rule: identify the writer before trusting the absence of an entry. The wrong fix it nearly produced (a TTY guard) was dropped before shipping.

summary: pg-test-db.sh binds a fixed port (55432) with no isolation between concurrent runs, cluster-wide or cross-repo, and the failures it produces look exactly like a real regression. Verifying an unrelated DDL-checksum fix, verify.sh's pg-test lane failed with asyncpg.exceptions.InternalServerError: tuple concurrently updated on GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA tabsii TO <role> -- a different set of tests every run (32, then 4, then 27), with every individual failing test passing 100% in isolation. Two wrong theories were tried first: system memory/swap (swap was full, but vmstat si/so showed ~0 active paging -- a red herring from a long session, not the cause) and inherent Postgres flakiness. ps aux found the real cause: a second verify.sh running concurrently, first from another local worktree with uncommitted work, then -- after that one finished and the failure recurred with yet another shifting error set -- from a completely different repo (biffo-template, a different Claude Code session). BIFFO_PG_PORT defaults to 55432 everywhere with no per-repo or per-worktree scoping, and Postgres roles (CREATE ROLE/GRANT) are cluster-wide, so even separate logical databases in the same cluster race on shared catalogs like pg_shdepend. Concurrent agent sessions across the whole estate are exactly the working mode this project runs in, so this was never a rare collision -- it was waiting to be hit
surfacedIn: tabsii-platform pg-test lane, while landing an unrelated fix; root cause in biffo-template scripts/pg-test-db.sh
fixesIn: biffo-template scripts/pg-test-db.sh (shared to every instance/sibling/plugin via core-manifest.json + shared-files.json)

summary: A repo-wide find-and-replace edited already-applied, checksum-tracked DDL, and every local and CI gate was green because the checksums live in the deployed database. Renumbering an instance's ADRs rewrote the citation everywhere it appeared -- including comments inside 21 db/imports/tabsii/*.sql modules that had already been applied. _run_ddl_import records a sha256 per applied file in ddl_import_history and hard-fails on any change, so the next deploy died on a checksum mismatch. Editing a COMMENT was enough: the hash is over the whole file, and the natural mental model ('it is only a comment, the SQL is unchanged') is wrong in a way nothing states. verify.sh, 3136 pytest, the 367-test real-Postgres RLS lane and every CI check passed on the offending PR. Three compounding failures made it expensive rather than annoying: (1) nothing pre-merge can see it, because the source of truth is a running database; (2) the poisoned branch then failed FIVE consecutive deploys over 2h25m, four of them innocent PRs by other people who each saw their own change 'break the deploy'; (3) the red deploy went unnoticed for two hours because five workflows run on a merge to dev and `gh run list --limit 3` shows none of them is Deploy Application -- so 'dev CI green' was reported, truthfully, while the deploy was red. AGENTS.md section 6 does say to confirm 'the CI (and any deploy workflow)'; the parenthetical is the whole instruction and it was read past.
surfacedIn: tabsii-platform dev deploy (5 consecutive failures, 10:43-13:08 on 2026-08-02)
fixesIn: fixed: tabsii-platform#514 restored all 21 files to their applied bytes (verified per file against the pre-change blob, not assumed). Guard added upstream in biffo-template services/api/tests/test_ddl_import_immutability.py -- any db/imports/**/*.sql present on the base branch must be byte-identical to it; new files unconstrained. Proven against the real defect by replaying the exact edit, which fails with an actionable message. The guard carries its own not-vacuous test, because it skips entirely in the template (no db/imports/) and a guard that only ever skips is indistinguishable from no guard.

summary: The error-branch coverage gate's verdict depends on a module's TEST STYLE, not on whether its error branches are tested. scripts/error_branch_coverage.py reads coverage.json, and coverage loses the trace on everything after the first `await` against a real in-memory aiosqlite engine: in lms_media.py line 201 (`await _brand_tenant(...)`) is recorded executed and line 205, four lines later in the same function, is not. Four `except` branches that WERE exercised -- the tests asserted the 502s and the 400 and passed -- were reported as 'added with no test exercising them'. The gate was not wrong to say so; there was no evidence. The split is estate-wide and measurable: test_fdd_admin.py uses the real-engine pattern (module at 65%), test_lead_stage.py uses a fake session (100%, with five awaits of its own). Two consequences: the ratchet will keep forcing baseline growth for genuinely-tested code, eroding the thing it measures; and per-module coverage percentages are not comparable across modules differing only in fixture style. Worked around in one module by moving the error tests to a fake session (61% -> 84%); the instrument is unchanged.
surfacedIn: tabsii-platform#467 CI, building LMS v1 M4

summary: A drift guard's character class silently narrowed what it guarded, and the gap held for a month. test_evidence_bucket_prefixes.py scans for S3 key prefixes with f"([a-z_]+)/\{ -- no hyphen -- so `onboarding-documents/`, granted in Terraform since 0011 M4, was ABSENT from CODE_PREFIXES and checked by nothing. The scanner could not match it, so its absence read as 'no such prefix exists' rather than 'not guarded'. Found only because the next prefix being added (course_materials/) prompted reading the regex rather than trusting it. The guard's own docstring already records it narrowing once before, when a line filter on `storage_key`/`_key =` missed `sealed/`. Same shape twice: a pattern written against the examples in front of the author, then treated as coverage. Widened to [a-z_-]+ and the missing row added; fail-first proven by removing the row and watching the drift test fail with an assertion the OLD regex could not have produced.

summary: A commit message that MENTIONS a CI-skip token skips CI. GitHub scans the whole message, not the subject, so prose in a body explaining the marker suppresses every workflow for that push. The commit *implementing* the sibling scaffold's deliberate marker (#1075) described itself in its own body and zero runs were created. Nothing about the symptom points at the cause: the PR sat BLOCKED on required checks that could never arrive, gh run list --branch <it> was empty while every other branch got runs normally, and closing and reopening the PR did not help — only amending the message and force-pushing did. The estate is now more exposed to this, not less, because the #1065 fix deliberately puts that token in every sibling scaffold commit, so any future commit or PR body discussing it is a candidate. cost ~25m

A latent lint error on a file nobody had ever staged silently aborted the first commit that touched it — and git push then reported success having pushed nothing. commitlint.config.js has failed eslint's no-undef on module since it was written: it is CommonJS by necessity, and the flat config had no override for it. That was invisible because pnpm run lint does not cover root tool configs, so the error only fires through lint-staged, which runs eslint on any staged *.js — and nobody had ever staged that file. The first editor inherits an abort they did not cause, from a rule they did not break, on a file the repo's own lint script calls clean. The abort was then masked exactly as AGENTS.md §4 describes: git rev-list --count origin/dev..HEAD said 0 while the push printed [new branch]. The generalisation is the useful part: a check that only ever runs on changed files has never been run against the files nobody changes, so its verdict on them is unknown rather than passing. cost ~10m

Writing them took one session; the manual instruction had been re-executed indefinitely and only catches the run someone remembers to do it on. summary: A wait loop that polls for the ABSENCE of pending work reads a transient empty set as completion. `until [ "$(gh pr checks N | grep -c pending)" = 0 ]; do sleep; done` exited immediately after `gh pr update-branch`, because GitHub drops the superseded check runs before registering the new ones — so for a few seconds there are ZERO checks, `pending` is 0, and the loop reports the same thing it would report for a fully green PR. The caller then proceeds to merge on a PR whose CI has not started. Nothing distinguishes 'all checks passed' from 'no checks exist yet' in that condition, which is the estate's dominant failure shape (a gate passing because it cannot run) reproduced inside the agent's own tooling rather than in CI. The fix is to require a POSITIVE signal: at least one check present AND every check concluded, never merely the absence of a negative. Same session, same loop, a second bug: `until cmd; [ $? -eq 0 ] || [ $? -eq 1 ] && ! echo ...` has precedence that never terminates, and burned a full 10-minute timeout doing nothing. Together ~12 minutes. Worth generalising because every session hand-rolls this loop — there is no shared wait-for-checks helper anywhere in the repo, so each agent reinvents it and gets it wrong differently, and the failure direction is always the dangerous one (proceed early) rather than the safe one (wait too long)
surfacedIn: agent tooling — ad-hoc `until` loops around `gh pr checks`, while clearing the 13-repo shared-sync queue
fixesIn: not fixed — no shared helper exists; recorded under 'what needs more thought'

summary: `2>/dev/null` on a `git fetch` discarded the one error that mattered, and the fail-open ran three levels deep. shared-sync's diff check ran `git fetch origin --prune --quiet 2>/dev/null`; a clone whose refspec is pinned to a branch the remote no longer has -- a --single-branch clone of `main` after the main->dev migration -- fails with `fatal: couldn't find remote ref refs/heads/main` and therefore PRUNES NOTHING, so the dead refs/remotes/origin/main survives the call. Everything downstream then read a ref the remote does not have: every shared file resolved against a frozen commit, so the repo reported DRIFTED when the truth was that nobody could read it, and `--check` exited 0 having counted it -- into the daily dashboard, where 0 renders as OK. Three distinct wrong answers (silenced error, phantom drift, green check) from one redirection. The general rule: `2>/dev/null` on a command whose failure changes the meaning of everything after it is not noise suppression, it is deleting the evidence. Suppress specific expected errors, never the channel. Fixed by capturing the error, reporting `cannot fetch` with git's own message and the clone's path, and making `--check` exit 1 for any repo it could not read -- their drift is unknown, not clean, which is the same shape as protection-audit.sh skipping a repo with no `dev` (#1145)
surfacedIn: biffo-template scripts/shared-sync.sh; observed against biffo-runners and tabsii-data-model-design

summary: A confident wrong diagnosis costs more than a blunt one, and error messages that name the LAST step attempted rather than the FIRST thing wrong manufacture them. shared-sync's ship phase ran four `git -C "$wt"` calls against a staged worktree that had vanished; each emitted `fatal: cannot change to '<path>': No such file or directory`, and the run reported `push failed: <that fatal>`. So the headline said push, and the detail said directory -- and the actual condition was a phase-1/phase-2 lifecycle problem in neither. I wrote TWO fixes on that reading (an existence check on `git worktree add`, a missing-ref check in the base resolver), both landing on things that were provably not the cause -- the add had been checked since #856, and the ship path takes its base from `gh repo view`, not the resolver -- and threw both away. What eventually worked was reproducing the clone shape end to end in a temp estate rather than reasoning from the message. Two rules worth carrying: an error should name the precondition that failed, not the operation that noticed; and when a message has sent you to a wrong layer twice, stop fixing and start reproducing. The cause is STILL unknown (#1160); what shipped (#1161) is a guard that makes the failure state its own name, which is worth having regardless of which mechanism removes the worktree

H4's primary outcome metric went blind and nothing failed, because the field that records the blindness was reported next to it and never asserted on. `gates.share` is computed over CLASSIFIED failing steps; a step whose name no STEP_KINDS pattern matches is counted as `unclassified` and dropped from the ratio. Dropping it is RIGHT for the ratio -- a default of `false` would improve the headline every time CI grew an unseen step -- but it means the denominator can shrink silently. On 2026-08-03, 12 of 17 estate failing steps were unclassified, all in tabsii-platform and all ordinary names (Apply DDL imports x5, Error-branch coverage x3, Initialise database schema x2, Sync portal to S3, ADR numbering guard). The dashboard read 80% locally-catchable; over all 17 steps the honest figure was 47%, with H4's review two days away. It also flattered the previous day's standup result: locallyCatchable fell 13->4, read as a win for putting the RLS lane on the local gate -- the RLS half was real (9 steps genuinely gone) but a 12-step cohort left the denominator at the same moment, so the improvement was smaller than the headline. This is the estate's most-repeated shape one level out: a check that cannot evaluate an input silently shrinks its own scope and reports the remainder as the whole -- the same defect as protection-audit.sh skipping repos with no `dev` (#1145) and shared-files.json distributing only what is already listed (#1108), except that here it was the DENOMINATOR that shrank rather than the repo list. Fixed three ways: patterns for all six shapes, each classified from what the step RUNS rather than what it is called (Apply DDL imports sounds local and is `aws lambda invoke`; Error-branch coverage sounds heavy and is a Python script finishing in seconds); `unclassifiedNames` in the snapshot so the failure can say WHICH patterns to write instead of sending the reader back to the jobs API; and scripts/classification-audit.mjs as a sixth estate audit failing the daily run above a 20% threshold. Not zero, deliberately -- a new step name is normal churn and a guard red every morning stops being read. RECURRENCE of the fail-open/reported-zero class
